finding.claim: GET /rss passes the unvalidated query parameter params[:u] to URI.open, letting any client make the server fetch an arbitrary URL and read back the first 400 bytes of the response (full-read SSRF).
finding.source: params[:u] from the query string of GET /rss (app.rb:7-8)
finding.sink: URI.open(params[:u]).read at app.rb:8 (open-uri performing an HTTP request); response body reflected via data[0, 400] at app.rb:9

trace.note: get "/rss" route; reachable by any client, no auth
params[:u] passed unmodified to URI.open, which issues the request and follows redirects
first 400 bytes of the response body returned to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: None. No scheme allowlist, no host or IP allowlist, no private/loopback/link-local blocking, no DNS pinning, no port restriction, no redirect control. Impact: reach internal services and cloud metadata (e.g. 169.254.169.254) with reflected response. Side note outside SSRF: open-uri falls back to Kernel#open for scheme-less input, enabling local file read and possibly pipe command execution on Ruby versions that support it.

verdict.guard_found: none. The only host check is TRUSTED.include?(uri.host) at app.rb:14, but it sits in the /trusted route (app.rb:12-16), not on the /rss path. /rss (app.rb:7-9) passes params[:u] straight to URI.open at line 8 with no scheme, host, IP, or redirect validation.
verdict.reason: The query parameter params[:u] at app.rb:7-8 is attacker-controlled and reaches URI.open unvalidated, and the first 400 bytes of the fetched body are returned at app.rb:9; the allowlist at app.rb:14 guards only the separate /trusted route, so the SSRF stands.
